title: James Cook Creates Stunning Art Using Only a Typewriter
summary: Most artists use paintbrushes or pencils. James Cook uses a typewriter. The 29-year-old Londoner creates detailed artworks by pressing keys on vintage typewriters — he owns over 100 of them. Cook discovered typewriter art in high school when a project challenged students to make art with technology. He found Paul Smith, an American artist with cerebral palsy who couldn't hold a pen, so he used a typewriter. Cook tried it and was instantly hooked. He became an architect but kept making typewriter art on the side. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he turned it into a full-time career. Today, he has created more than 350 artworks, including cityscapes of London and Tokyo and portraits of Frida Kahlo and Vincent van Gogh. His most popular piece is a drawing of Wimbledon's Centre Court. Made with a 1932 typewriter, it took about four weeks and over one million keystrokes. Since appearing online in June 2026, it has been viewed more than eight million times. Cook plans each piece carefully. He makes a layout using photos and software, then types a faint guide with a dry ribbon. Next, he switches to a fresh ink ribbon and builds the image keystroke by keystroke. He changes how hard he hits the keys to create light and dark areas. He uses capital 'E's for buildings and windows, and '@' for shadows. Each artwork takes a week to three months. He sells originals for $4,000 to $40,000 and prints starting at around $110. 'I actually think the limitations are what make it so exciting,' Cook says. 'You have to work with a fixed set of tools, albeit the 45 keys of a typical typewriter, and that forces you to think differently. It's incredibly satisfying.'
why_it_matters: Cook's story shows that an old, limited tool can be the base of a real career — a useful reminder for 12-14 year-olds choosing subjects and wondering whether hobbies can lead anywhere in a digital, AI-heavy economy.

background_read: Typewriters were invented in the 1800s and were the standard writing machine until personal computers took over in the 1980s. Almost as soon as they existed, people discovered that the keys could be used to make pictures, and the hobby became known as typewriter art.

Paul Smith, the artist Cook found while still at school, was an American who had cerebral palsy — a condition that affects movement and muscle control — so he could not hold a pen or a brush. He typed pictures for decades and is remembered as one of the most important typewriter artists.

Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter known for bold self-portraits, and Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch painter whose vivid works, such as The Starry Night, are among the most famous in the world. Wimbledon's Centre Court is the main court of the Wimbledon tennis tournament, the oldest tennis championship in the world, played in London.
Cook's 1932 machine is an example of a vintage object — something old that is valued for its age and design rather than being thrown away when newer models appear.

perspectives.description: Cook turns a strict limit — 45 keys and one colour of ink — into detailed, recognisable images, and his work has reached millions of viewers. His path also honours Paul Smith, an artist whose disability pushed him towards an unexpected medium.

The art world's prices mean few people can ever own an original: at $4,000 to $40,000, this is a luxury market. Some critics also argue that viral popularity built on a novelty tool can fade fast once the surprise wears off.

Typewriter art is not new — it has existed since typewriters did, and it survives today in forms such as ASCII art and pixel art. Artists have long found that technical constraints, rather than freedom, often push creative work in more interesting directions.

As digital tools and AI image generators make pictures instantly, handmade work with a physical machine may gain value for being slow, imperfect and clearly human. The open question is how artists like Cook keep earning from that difference as the technology changes around them.
